video:video.video:title: Why Chile Is So Long and Thin
video:video.video:description: Chile is thin because the Andes mountains run down its whole eastern side, leaving a narrow strip between the peaks and the Pacific. It is long because nearly four centuries of conquest, war and treaties added land to the north and south: the occupation of Araucanía, the Strait of Magellan, the War of the Pacific and the 1902 Andes arbitration with Argentina.

video:video.video:title: Why Is Greenland Icy and Iceland Green?
video:video.video:description: Greenland is about 80% ice because the cold East Greenland Current flows down its coast from the Arctic, while Iceland is warmed by the North Atlantic and Irminger currents. The swapped-sounding names come from two Vikings a century apart: Flóki named Iceland after a bad winter, and Erik the Red named Greenland to attract settlers.

video:video.video:title: Why Does Brazil Speak Portuguese? The 1494 Line
video:video.video:description: Brazil speaks Portuguese because of the Treaty of Tordesillas (7 June 1494), which split newly found lands along a line 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands: west for Castile (Spain), east for Portugal. The eastern bulge of South America fell on Portugal's side, and Pedro Álvares Cabral claimed Brazil for Portugal in 1500.

video:video.video:title: How Istanbul Ended Up on Two Continents
video:video.video:description: Istanbul is on two continents because it grew on both shores of the Bosphorus, the narrow strait that divides Europe from Asia. Greek settlers founded Chalcedon on the Asian shore first, then Byzantium on the better European site opposite; the city later spread across the strait, and today about two in three residents live on the European side.
